decision.explanation: An antiderivative is arcsin(x/5). Thus the integral equals arcsin(1/2) − arcsin(−1/2) = π/6 − (−π/6) = π/3.

after.name: Question 1
after.worked_solution:
Let's rewrite our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-5/2}^{5/2}\frac{\text{d}x}{\sqrt{25-{x}^{2}}}\, & ={\int }_{-5/2}^{5/2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{25\cdot (1-{x}^{2}/25)}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{5}{\int }_{-5/2}^{5/2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}/25}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{5}{\int }_{-5/2}^{5/2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-(x/5)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse sine,

$$
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\text{d}u=\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(u)+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have ${(\frac{x}{5})}^{2}.$

So, let's substitute $u=\frac{x}{5}.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{5}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=5\,\text{d}u.
$$

Before substituting, we use the table below to change the limits from $x$ to $u.$

| $x$ | $-\frac{5}{2}$ | $\frac{5}{2}$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $-\frac{1}{2}$ | $\frac{1}{2}$ |

Using the above, we can now write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-5/2}^{5/2}\frac{\text{d}x}{\sqrt{25-{x}^{2}}} & =\frac{1}{5}{\int }_{-5/2}^{5/2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-(x/5)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{5}{\int }_{-1/2}^{1/2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\cdot (5\,\text{d}u) \\  & ={\int }_{-1/2}^{1/2}\frac{\text{d}u}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}} \\  & =\operatorname{arcsin}⁡u{|}_{-1/2}^{1/2} \\  & =\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(\frac{1}{2})-\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(-\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{6}+\frac{\pi }{6} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{3}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

after.worked_solution:
Note that we can rewrite this integral as

$$
\int \frac{8\,\text{d}x}{|8x|\sqrt{(8x)^{2}-1}}=8\int \frac{\text{d}x}{|8x|\sqrt{(8x)^{2}-1}}.
$$

This integral now resembles the basic one for $\text{arcsec},$

$$
\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\text{d}u=\text{arcsec}(u)+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of $u$ as the variable, we have $8x.$

So, let's substitute $u=8x.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=8\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{8}\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}8\int \frac{1}{|8x|\sqrt{(8x)^{2}-1}}\text{d}x & =8\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\cdot (\frac{1}{8}\text{d}u) \\  & =\int \frac{\text{d}u}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}} \\  & =\text{arcsec }u+C \\  & =\text{arcsec}(8x)+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

after.worked_solution:
Note that we can rewrite this integral as

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}x}{5|x|\sqrt{25{x}^{2}-1}}=\int \frac{\text{d}x}{|5x|\sqrt{(5x)^{2}-1}}.
$$

This integral now resembles the basic one for $\text{arcsec},$

$$
\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\text{d}u=\text{arcsec}(u)+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of $u$ as the variable, we have $5x.$

So, let's substitute $u=5x.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=5\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{5}\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{5|x|\sqrt{25{x}^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{|5x|\sqrt{(5x)^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\cdot (\frac{1}{5}\text{d}u) \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\int \frac{\text{d}u}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\text{arcsec }u+C \\  & =\frac{\text{arcsec}(5x)}{5}+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 4
after.worked_solution:
This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse tangent,

$$
\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\text{d}u=\operatorname{arctan}⁡u+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have $5{x}^{2}=(\sqrt{5}x)^{2}.$

Thus, let's substitute $u=\sqrt{5}x.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\sqrt{5}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{1+5{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{1+(\sqrt{5}x)^{2}}\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\cdot (\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\text{d}u) \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{5}}{5}\operatorname{arctan}⁡u+C \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{5}}{5}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\sqrt{5}x)+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

content.worked_solution:
This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse tangent,

$$
\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\text{d}u=\operatorname{arctan}⁡u+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have $5{x}^{2}=(\sqrt{5}x)^{2}.$

Thus, let's substitute $u=\sqrt{5}x.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\sqrt{5}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{1+5{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{1+(\sqrt{5}x)^{2}}\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\cdot (\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\text{d}u) \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{5}}{5}\operatorname{arctan}⁡u+C \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{5}}{5}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\sqrt{5}x)+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=3\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{3}\,\text{d}u.
